Council Approves Plan to Close Three City Libraries Despite Fierce Opposition

The decision, passed by a single vote, will save an estimated £1.2m a year.

By Hannah Whitfield, Local Democracy Reporter
20 October 2026

Three of Northfield's seven branch libraries will close next spring after councillors voted narrowly on Monday evening to approve a cost-cutting plan that campaigners described as "a quiet loss that will be felt for a generation".

The proposal, which passed by 24 votes to 23 after more than four hours of debate, will close the branches in Eastgate, Millbrook and Hollins Park. The council says the move will save around £1.2m a year at a time when it faces a budget gap of almost £19m.

Councillor Rebecca Shaw, the cabinet member for communities, told the chamber that the decision had been "the hardest of my time in office". She said the authority had protected the central library and the four busiest branches, which together account for more than eighty percent of all visits and loans.

Advertisement

"Nobody in this room wanted to be here," Ms Shaw said. "But the money we receive from central government has fallen in real terms for a decade, and the law requires us to set a balanced budget. If we do not make these savings now, we will be making far deeper cuts to adult social care next year."

Opposition members argued that the council had not properly considered alternatives. Councillor David Mensah proposed reducing opening hours at all seven branches instead of closing three, an amendment that was defeated by two votes. He said the closures would fall hardest on older residents and families without cars, because the nearest remaining library to Hollins Park is a forty-minute bus journey away.

A petition opposing the plan gathered more than 9,000 signatures in six weeks. Around sixty residents attended the meeting, many holding hand-written signs, and several were asked to leave the public gallery after interrupting the debate.

Margaret Ellison, who has volunteered at the Eastgate branch for eleven years, said the library was more than a place to borrow books. "It is where people come to get help filling in forms, to use a computer, to keep warm, to talk to someone," she said. "For some of our regulars, we are the only conversation they have all week."

The council has said it will explore whether community groups could take over the buildings, as has happened in several other towns. A consultation on that option is expected to open in January. Officers told the meeting that the home delivery service, which brings books to housebound residents, would be expanded to cover the affected areas.

Library staff at the three branches will be offered roles elsewhere in the service where possible. The trade union representing the staff said it was "deeply disappointed" and would be seeking urgent talks about the number of posts at risk.

The closures are due to take effect on 1 April. A final decision on the future of the buildings themselves will be made by the cabinet in the summer.
